name: PT Astra Otoparts Tbk

frontmatter.title: Astra Otoparts - an autoparts franchise priced as a break-up
frontmatter.summary: An Astra-controlled autoparts maker whose share price is close to the sum of its net cash and the book value of its Japanese joint-venture stakes, so the operating business trades at a small multiple of its cash earnings. This update answers Gaikindo's October print: wholesales ran above the nine-month pace, the fourth-quarter slowdown we assumed at initiation did not arrive, and FY2026E revenue growth rises to 15.0%. Target Rp4,852, BUY.
thesis: The share price is close to net cash plus the book value of the associate and joint-venture stakes, so the operating autoparts business is being valued at a small fraction of its cash earnings and replacement cost.

Segment mix is shifting toward manufacturing; revenue is growing at a double-digit pace but gross margin is lower, and our base case holds the observed margin rather than assuming a recovery. The October wholesale print confirms the volume leg of that growth [S14].

The local-content step-up is written for electric vehicles, a small share of revenue today, so we treat it as a free option rather than the reason to own the shares; the carrier is the aftermarket distribution network and the OEM scale behind it.
Cash conversion is strong, the balance sheet carries net cash rather than net debt, and the board has paid out roughly half of earnings through the cycle.
The main risk is now a normalisation of the car cycle in 2027 plus imported Chinese components compressing aftermarket margins further; both are in our bear case [S14][S12].

catalysts.event: Gaikindo November wholesales data and the run-rate into the year-end target
Higher minimum local-content threshold takes effect for battery electric vehicles
FY2026 audited results and the board's dividend recommendation
Annual general meeting approving the FY2026 final dividend

open_items: IDX board and notation status unverified — no IDX announcement or KSEI registry extract held; no entry or exit assumption in this report depends on it.

blocks.text: **What changed, and why.** This update answers Gaikindo's October wholesale print, and it removes the premise the initiation rested on. National car wholesales reached 760,476 units in the ten months to October, of which 81,482 came in October alone — up 31.2% on October 2025 and 2.4% on September — with retail sales of 758,653 units over the ten months [S14]. October therefore ran above the nine-month monthly average, and the full-year target of 850,000 now needs a November-December rate far below the October print. The size of the revision should be stated plainly, because the headline number moved further than the substance. The article's ten-month growth rate is not usable: struck against a comparative that is really the nine-month base, it overstates the market at about thirty-five per cent, and the correct ten-month rate on the article's own monthly units is about twenty-two per cent (F44, F48) [S14]. Against that, the FY2026E revenue growth we published was thirteen-point-seven per cent, with the fourth quarter held at ten per cent; we now hold the fourth quarter at fifteen per cent, the nine-month rate, so the full-year rate rises to 15.0% — about one and a third points — and the target moves from the published level by less than one per cent, to Rp4,852 against Rp3,220. Nothing else in the model moves: gross margin stays at the nine-month mix-driven level, and the associate income line, capex, working capital, the payout and the cost of capital are unchanged. The target is a total return of 58.5%, and the rating is unchanged at BUY.

We maintain coverage of PT Astra Otoparts at BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp4,852, a total return of 58.5% from the Rp3,220 price in our data pack. The target is the weighted output of a free-cash-flow DCF at fifty per cent, a P/E cross-check at thirty and an EV/EBITDA cross-check at twenty, with the base case at Rp4,791 and the probability-weighted scenario value at Rp4,852.

The variant view is about what the market is actually charging for. At the current capitalisation of IDR15,519.5bn, the company is valued at little more than the sum of its balance-sheet liquidity and the carrying value of its stakes in Denso Indonesia, GS Battery, Akebono Brake, Kayaba and a dozen smaller component ventures. The balance sheet at 30 September 2026 holds cash of IDR5,087.8bn against total borrowings of IDR560.5bn, and the associates and joint ventures carry at IDR2,327.7bn and IDR5,123.6bn respectively at that date [S3]. Those stakes earned IDR1,176.9bn of equity-accounted profit in FY2025, so they are not a dormant asset [S5]. Strip the cash and the stakes out and the market is ascribing a multiple of barely two times cash earnings to a business that generates IDR1,853.2bn of EBITDA on IDR19,906.8bn of revenue — cheap enough that the debate is about whether the discount should exist at all, not about the price of the operating franchise.

The operating evidence is not gloomy. Nine-month revenue to September reached IDR17,021.9bn, with manufacturing revenue of IDR9,180.5bn and trading revenue of IDR7,841.3bn, and profit attributable to shareholders of IDR1,799.9bn [S3]. Management describes the growth as demand-led, from original-equipment component volumes across cars, motorcycles and commercial vehicles and from a fuller aftermarket range sold through the retail network [S2]. The company also guided for growth above the industry rate in 2027 [S7].

What moves the value is therefore narrow and identifiable. First, national car wholesales: Gaikindo recorded 760,476 units in the ten months to October against a full-year target of 850,000 [S14][S8]. Second, gross margin mix: manufacturing carries a far lower margin than trading, so the faster the manufacturing line grows the more group margin dilutes [S3]. Third, equity-accounted income from the joint ventures, which is close to half of pretax profit — IDR1,176.9bn on IDR2,639.5bn — and is the single largest reason our DCF value sits above the market price [S5]. We take each in turn below.

The stock is not without reasons to be cheap. The free float is 19.9% with Astra International holding 80 per cent of the shares, and the stock trades about IDR11.4bn a day [S0]. A minority holder is buying a controlled company's cash flows at a discount, and that discount is the risk as much as the opportunity.

Astra Otoparts makes and distributes parts for cars and motorcycles through two reportable segments. The trading segment buys, warehouses and distributes replacement parts through a network of 49 main dealers, 28 sales offices and more than 15,000 independent parts shops, supplemented by 673 modern retail outlets trading as Shop & Drive, Super Shop & Drive, Astra Otoservice, Shop & Bike and Aspira Motoquick [S2]. The manufacturing segment supplies original equipment to vehicle assemblers and the original-equipment service channel, through owned plants and through joint ventures with Japanese component makers [S4].

The mix matters more than the headline. In FY2025 the trading segment booked IDR9,340.8bn of external revenue and manufacturing IDR10,565.9bn, so manufacturing is the larger half [S4]. Trading earned a gross margin several times the manufacturing margin, however, and manufacturing reaches that revenue on a base that also includes intersegment sales [S4]. The segment growing fastest is therefore the one that dilutes group margin, and the nine-month results show exactly that [S3].

The product range is broad rather than deep in any single category: batteries, chains and filters, rubber and metal components, jacks and tools, plastic components, pistons, wheel rims, frame chassis and transmission parts [S0]. Several subsidiaries act as export production bases for Japanese, American and European customers, and the group sells into more than 50 countries [S4]. Electrification is being handled as an extension rather than a replacement: management argues that shock absorbers, brakes and many general parts do not change between combustion and electric vehicles, while separately developing electric-vehicle-specific components and a charging business of 71 Astra Otopower units [S7].

The strategic plan for 2027 is explicit: grow above the industry rate, add around 30 modern retail stores, deepen the aftermarket range and the digital Astra Otoshop channel, and expand electric-vehicle components and charging infrastructure [S7]. That is a continuation of the current model rather than a new one, which is why we model it as revenue growth on a stable margin rather than as a margin story [S7].

Ownership is central to how the equity should be valued. PT Astra International Tbk owns 80 per cent of the shares and the balance is in public hands [S4]. The controlling group is also the customer base: Astra Honda Motor and Astra Daihatsu Motor take a large share of manufacturing output, which we return to in the governance section [S5]. Below the listed company sit the consolidated manufacturing subsidiaries and, alongside them, the equity-accounted ventures — Denso Indonesia at an effective stake in the mid-twenties, and GS Battery, Akebono Brake Astra, Kayaba Indonesia and Inti Ganda Perdana at or near half ownership [S5].

The demand pool is Indonesian vehicle production and the vehicle parc. Car wholesales reached 760,476 units in the ten months of 2026, and Gaikindo targets 850,000 units for the full year [S14][S8]. The motorcycle market is larger and steadier: sales passed the five million mark by September and the industry association expects a full-year range whose upper end is 6.7 million units [S9]. Astra's own framing, in its annual report, is that four-wheeler demand was the volatile part of the market while two-wheelers were relatively stagnant [S4].

The arithmetic of the target has flipped, and that is the substance of this update. To reach 850,000 units after 760,476 in ten months, the industry needs a November-December run-rate well below the October print of 81,482 units [S14][S8]. At initiation the same arithmetic read the other way: after nine months the target required a fourth-quarter rate far below the year-to-date pace, which we took as a warning that the market would have to slow, and we held the fourth quarter's revenue accordingly. October did not slow. It ran above the nine-month monthly average, 31.2% ahead of October 2025 and 2.4% ahead of September, and retail sales of 758,653 units over the ten months show the demand reaching buyers rather than sitting in dealer stock [S14]. The target is now a floor rather than a stretch, and the risk we carry in section five — a fourth quarter that does not deliver — has been answered for one of its months.

One caution on the data, because it changes the size of the step we take. The article's headline ten-month growth rate is not usable: its comparative of 561,405 units is essentially the nine-month base implied by the 679,020 nine-month print and its 21.0% growth rate, and it leaves almost no October 2025 sales at all against the article's own 62,090 units for that month [S14][S8]. We use the monthly units and the nine-month growth rate, not the headline, and the revenue step-up in section three is sized to the former.

Regulation matters, but less than the headline suggests, and we scale it to the revenue it can reach. The minimum domestic content requirement is set by Perpres 79/2023 and steps to 60 per cent for 2027 to 2029 and to eighty per cent from 2030 — but the rule is written for battery electric vehicles, not for the internal-combustion content that is the overwhelming majority of this company's revenue [S13]. The company treats electrification as an extension of the existing range rather than a replacement, with a charging business of 71 units and components common to both powertrains [S7]. So the local-content step is a real but small option: it can convert imported electric-vehicle content into addressable demand for a maker with existing plants and original- equipment qualification, provided the local industry can scale, and the same policy discussion warns that a threshold without enforcement and without demand simply raises assemblers' costs [S13]. We therefore do not treat it as the industry's dominant variable; the car cycle and the aftermarket import threat are larger.

Competition is two-sided. On the original-equipment side the barriers are qualification cycles, tooling investment and quality consistency; the relationship is sticky but the customer holds the pricing power, which is why manufacturing margins are thin [S4]. On the aftermarket side the barriers are distribution density and brand, and here the threat is imported product, particularly from China, which the industry association acknowledges as the sector's central competitive challenge even as it argues that the electric transition does not eliminate the parts market [S12]. The company's own answer is authenticity, quality and service reliability rather than price [S4].

Our view of the moat is that it is real but narrow, and that it sits in distribution rather than in technology. The parts-shop network, the dealer relationships and the retail footprint are expensive to replicate and give the trading segment a gross margin several times the manufacturing margin [S3]. The manufacturing side has scale and long-standing Japanese partners, but it earns a supplier's return, and the joint ventures that hold the best technology are not consolidated [S5]. That is why we value the operating business on cash flow with a fade rather than as a compounder with a widening moat, and why the associate portfolio is carried at book rather than capitalised at a growth multiple.

Autoparts economics split cleanly between the original-equipment channel and the replacement
aftermarket. Original-equipment supply is a volume business with thin margins, long qualification
cycles and annual price-downs negotiated by the assembler. The aftermarket is a distribution business:
margins are wider, demand is tied to the vehicle parc rather than to new sales, and the constraint is
shelf space and logistics reach rather than engineering. Companies that own both channels use the
original-equipment relationship to seed brand acceptance and the aftermarket network to earn the
return. Vehicle electrification shifts the component list but leaves much of the chassis, braking and
suspension content in place.

Five forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate and partly internal, since several joint ventures are also suppliers [S5]. Buyer power is high in original equipment and lower in the aftermarket [S4]. Threat of new entrants is low in qualified original equipment and moderate in imported aftermarket parts [S12]. Substitutes are the electric powertrain, which removes engine and transmission content but not the rest [S12]. Rivalry is high and rising, with the trading segment competing on range and authenticity and manufacturing competing on cost and delivery [S4].

External influences are mostly macro. A weaker rupiah raises the cost of imported raw materials and finished parts, and the house macro deck projects the exchange rate at 18,350 to the dollar in 2027 [S15]. Interest rates matter less here than for most Indonesian names because the company holds net cash, but they matter for the cost of the working capital that funds inventory and receivables [S5]. The demand cycle is the swing factor, and it is cyclical rather than structural: the parc keeps growing even when new sales stall [S4].

One contradiction has to be stated rather than left implicit. The house macro deck sits in a balance-of-payments-pressure regime with a cautious risk appetite and an AVOID on Indonesian rate-sensitive consumer discretionary, and this report is a BUY [S15]. The deck's transmission is the rupiah and the funding leg: a weaker currency raises imported input costs, and a higher cost of capital compresses the multiple. This company is exposed to the first and barely to the second. It holds cash of IDR5,087.8bn against borrowings of IDR560.5bn at 30 September 2026, so its earnings are not geared to the policy rate, and its revenue is tied to the vehicle parc and the aftermarket rather than to consumer credit [S3]. The AVOID is a sector stance, not a name verdict. We therefore take the currency risk explicitly — it is in the cost base and in the bear case — and hold the sector warning in the multiple we apply rather than in the rating, because the name's own drivers (a net cash sheet, parc-driven demand, a 50.0% payout funded from free cash flow) override the sector tilt for this one name. Where the deck does bind, it binds on the price of imported components, and section five carries that.

The historical record is one of slow top-line growth and steady profitability until this year. Revenue moved from IDR18,579.9bn in FY2022 to IDR19,906.8bn in FY2025, a compound rate in the low single digits, while gross profit rose from IDR2,689.3bn to IDR3,366.2bn as the trading mix improved [S5]. Operating profit over the same span went from IDR957.4bn to IDR1,265.9bn [S5]. Then 2026 broke the pattern: nine-month revenue of IDR17,021.9bn and gross profit of IDR2,649.6bn are both well ahead of the comparable period, and profit attributable to shareholders reached IDR1,799.9bn [S3].

The first restatement a reader needs is depreciation. The data pack carries a D&A charge that is a small fraction of what the accounts show, because Indonesian filings present the cash-flow statement on the direct method and the depreciation sits in the notes rather than on a face line. From the notes, total depreciation and amortisation was IDR529.9bn in FY2022, IDR525.8bn in FY2023, IDR562.7bn in FY2024 and IDR587.2bn in FY2025, and IDR458.3bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S5][S6][S11]. We feed those into the model, which rebuilds EBITDA: FY2025 EBITDA is IDR1,853.2bn, an EBITDA margin of 9.3%, not the roughly seven per cent a pack-based calculation would show. Every margin statement in this report uses the restated figure.

The second structural point is that operating profit is not where the earnings are. In FY2025 the group earned IDR1,265.9bn of operating profit but IDR2,639.5bn of pretax profit, because below the operating result sit IDR1,162.7bn of non-operating income, of which IDR1,176.9bn is the equity-accounted share of associates and joint ventures, and IDR248.4bn of finance income [S5]. We model that equity income explicitly as an other non-operating item at IDR1,650.7bn, annualising a nine-month share-of-associates line that grew strongly year-on-year [S3]. The forecast path grows it twelve per cent in FY2027E — below the thirteen-point-four per cent FY2025 and seventeen per cent nine-month actual rates — then fades to six and a half per cent by FY2030E as the vehicle cycle normalises; a flat six per cent from the first forecast year, which an earlier draft carried, understated the line the LK actually shows [S5][S3]. Without it the model would understate earnings by close to half. The line is carried at its pre-tax equivalent so that it bears no tax: the LK deducts the associates' profit from the tax base because it arrives already taxed at the investee, and the model reproduces that by grossing the exempt share up at the operating rate, which leaves FY2026E parent net profit at IDR2,435.9bn and EPS at Rp505 rather than the roughly one-tenth lower figures a model that taxed the associate income a second time would print [S5].

Our forecast for FY2026 is revenue of IDR22,892.8bn, growth of 15.0%, built from the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter growing at about the nine-month rate: October wholesales reached 81,482 units, so the slowdown the target arithmetic implied when we initiated is no longer the most likely path [S14][S8]. The step up is deliberately smaller than the October unit rate, because AUTO's revenue grew more slowly than the car market over the nine months and November and December are unobserved. Gross margin is assumed at 15.6%, essentially the nine-month outcome, which is below the FY2025 level because manufacturing is now the faster-growing segment [S3]. Selling and administrative costs are held at 10.0% of revenue against a nine-month outcome slightly below that, leaving room for wage inflation and the planned store additions [S7]. The FY2025 comparative is the LK's own: selling costs of IDR1,054.5bn plus general and administrative costs of IDR1,072.3bn on net revenue of IDR19,906.8bn [S5]. The model's FY2025 opex line of IDR2,100.3bn is the data pack's and sits below that LK sum, so the restated FY2025 EBITDA of IDR1,853.2bn is slightly above the figure the LK lines imply (gross profit less selling and G&A plus D&A); the gap is in the history and is not carried into the forecast ratio we apply [S5]. The result is FY2026 operating profit of IDR1,282.0bn and EBITDA of IDR1,907.0bn, an EBITDA margin of 8.3% — below FY2025 not because we are cautious but because the mix and the realised gross margin say so.

Cash flow and the balance sheet are the strongest part of the story. Free cash flow to the firm was IDR1,184.9bn in FY2025 after capital expenditure of IDR544.4bn, and net profit converted to cash with little left in working capital [S5]. The nine-month capex figure of IDR445.6bn is running at a similar proportion of revenue [S3]. Working capital is modest at 7.0% of revenue, though it rose in the September balance sheet as payables and inventories built with manufacturing volume [S3]. Cash was IDR4,530.3bn against total debt of IDR597.5bn at the last year-end, and the September position is stronger still: cash and cash equivalents of IDR5,087.8bn against total borrowings of IDR560.5bn [S3].

One forecast convention needs stating here because it is visible in the valuation and not in the five-year table. Capex is held at the observed proportion of revenue through FY2030E, then rises to 4.1% of revenue by FY2035E. That is not a view that the company will become more capital-hungry in the ordinary sense; it is the terminal fade, explained in section four, which sets the return on new capital in the terminal year to the cost of capital instead of leaving the observed near-zero net reinvestment to compound forever [S5][S3]. The explicit years a reader can check against the company's own guidance are unchanged.

Earnings quality screens pass. The accruals ratio, measured as net profit less operating cash flow over average total assets, has been low in each of the last three years and was under two per cent in FY2025, so reported profit is being converted into cash rather than sitting in working capital [S5]. Working capital grew with volume rather than ahead of it, and neither of the usual divergence flags is present [S5]. The one flag that would matter at another company — related-party intensity — is present and large, at 34.8% of revenue and a similar share of purchases, but it is disclosed, reflected in the segment margins and structural to the Astra ecosystem [S5]. We treat it as a governance discount rather than as a manipulation signal, and discuss it in section six.

Capital allocation is conservative and predictable. The board paid a final FY2025 dividend of IDR819.4bn and declared a FY2026 interim of IDR349.5bn, and the payout has run near half of earnings [S3]. With capex at a low proportion of revenue and net cash on the balance sheet, the dividend is covered by free cash flow through the explicit forecast even in a weaker year, and the group has not needed capital markets since listing [S5].

We use a discounted free cash flow to the firm as the primary method, with a P/E cross-check and an EV/EBITDA cross-check. The reason is structural: this is an asset-backed industrial with low, observable capital intensity and a separately identifiable non-operating asset pool, so cash flow is the honest measure, while earnings multiples anchor the answer to what comparable parts businesses trade at. A sum-of-the-parts would also be defensible, but the operating segments share plants, customers and working capital, so a segment-level DCF would be false precision.

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck: a rupiah risk-free rate of 7.4%, a sovereign default spread of 1.6%, a mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5%, applied to an unlevered beta of 0.90, the industry default, since the company carries almost no debt and its own regression history is short. The result is a cost of equity of 12.0% and a WACC of 11.9%, inside the house band of eleven to thirteen per cent for rupiah names. Debt is 3.5% of the capital structure because the company holds net cash, so the WACC is effectively the cost of equity.

The tax line in the DCF is the operating rate, not the group's blended rate, and that distinction is worth stating because it is the one place where a consolidated number misleads. The LK's tax charge of IDR291.7bn is struck on pretax profit of IDR2,639.5bn after deducting the share of associates' net profit of IDR1,176.9bn, which arrives already taxed and is modelled outside EBIT [S5]. The rate borne by the operating business is therefore 19.9%, close to the theoretical rate on consolidated profit, and that is what the model applies to EBIT; taxing EBIT at the group's lower blended rate would overstate free cash flow and the target [S5].

The DCF produces an enterprise value of IDR12,187.2bn and an equity value per share of Rp4,904, with the terminal value accounting for 44.2% of the total, within the normal range for a ten-year explicit forecast. Three things drive that number and each is sourced. The explicit-period free cash flow grows from IDR763.5bn in FY2026E to IDR1,133.7bn in FY2035E on the revenue path set out in section three. The reinvestment need is low through those years: capex runs at 2.6% of revenue against D&A of 2.7%, so most of operating profit converts to cash.

The terminal value is where the growth has to be paid for, and we state the identity the house card requires: growth equals the reinvestment rate times the return on incremental capital. Through the forecast years the observed capex and working-capital path reinvests a shrinking share of NOPAT while revenue compounds, an implied incremental return far above anything an autoparts supplier sustains. We therefore fade it. From FY2031E capex rises to 4.1% of revenue by FY2035E, so that the terminal reinvestment rate — capex of IDR1,503.5bn less D&A of IDR1,024.4bn plus the working-capital build of IDR99.2bn, measured against terminal NOPAT — equals the growth rate of 4.0% divided by the cost of capital of 11.9% [S5][S3]. The terminal return on new capital is therefore the WACC, not the near-triple-digit incremental return the unfaded path implied. That is the fade the compounder card demands of a supplier whose moat section two calls real but narrow, and it is why the terminal value is the share of enterprise value shown above rather than the half a no-fade DCF would produce. The terminal growth rate itself stays at 4.0%, below the house cap and below the growth of the car parc, because the fade belongs in the reinvestment rate rather than in a growth rate cut to fit it.

The equity bridge is where this valuation differs from a simple operating-business DCF, and it is struck on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet the engine uses rather than the last year-end. To the enterprise value we add the net cash position: cash and cash equivalents of IDR5,087.8bn against total borrowings of IDR560.5bn, so cash exceeds debt and the net balance is positive and is added, not subtracted [S3]. We then deduct non-controlling interests of IDR1,245.8bn and add the carrying value of the associate and joint-venture investments at the same date, IDR2,327.7bn and IDR5,123.6bn [S3]. That treatment is the neutral one: the stakes earned IDR1,176.9bn last year, so book capitalises them on a single-digit multiple of their income, below the 8.0 times we apply to the group's own earnings and far below the peer median, and a buyer paying book is not paying up for them [S5]. The stakes are cash-backed, not an accrual: the FY2025 cash-flow statement reports IDR661.7bn of cash dividends received from associates and joint ventures, over half of the equity income booked that year [S5]. That is the proof the portfolio is not a dormant asset, and it is why we hold it at book with confidence rather than as a plug.

We carry book in every scenario, including the bull. At the 8.0 times we apply to the group's own earnings the portfolio would be worth a large multiple of its carrying value, an upside of several hundred rupiah a share that is not in the target because we cannot source a private-market price we can audit. It is stated in section five as an unmodelled upside, not folded into a bull value that would then be doing valuation work on an unsourced multiple. Their size is why section five also stresses the book as the place where the downside sits.

The bridge carries one more owned asset the operating cash flow does not value. Investment properties of IDR714.2bn sit on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet at carrying value; the rental income they earn is reported in the other-income line below EBIT, so the free cash flow we discount from operating profit does not capture it, and we add the asset at book rather than capitalising the rent separately [S3]. That is the same convention we apply to the associate and joint-venture stakes, and it is deliberately the conservative end of the treatment: book, not an appraised value.

Both cross-checks now sit below the DCF, the EV/EBITDA leg only marginally and the P/E leg by about a fifth, and the reason is knowable rather than mysterious. The P/E cross-check applies 8.0 times, the blend of the peer median and the company's own five-year average, to trailing parent earnings, giving Rp3,674, which is -25.1% against the DCF. The EV/EBITDA cross-check applies 6.2 times to trailing EBITDA of IDR1,853.2bn, which is the restated figure built on the LK's depreciation charge rather than the pack's, giving Rp4,744, or -3.3% against the DCF [S5]. The P/E cross-check capitalises parent earnings at a peer multiple that already embeds the market's current discount for Indonesian small and mid caps, and it is the leg that carries the associate income inside the metric; the EV/EBITDA leg is the closer of the two because it is struck on the restated operating profit and does not depend on the associate line at all.

We have therefore kept the weights rather than re-weighting toward the answer we prefer, and we flag the consequence: the target sits above both cross-checks, and a reader who does not accept the DCF's cash conversion should use the cross-check range as the honest downside.

The sensitivity tables show what matters, and they run in the right direction now that the terminal value is faded. A one percentage point change in the terminal growth rate moves the DCF value by more than a one point change in the WACC, because the terminal value is a large share of the answer; among the operating drivers a one point change in gross margin moves the target more than a one point change in revenue growth, since margin flows straight through to operating profit while growth also drags capex and working capital. The associate income line matters less to the DCF, because we carry the stakes at book rather than capitalising their earnings, but it matters a great deal to the P/E cross-check and therefore to the blended target.

What today's price implies is the most useful test, and the engine runs it explicitly: at Rp3,220 the reverse DCF solves to an implied FY2027E revenue growth rate of -15.1% on the same free-cash-flow model that produces our value, so the share price requires revenue to fall for a decade [S3]. There are only two readings. Either the market is wrong about the operating business, or it is not valuing the operating business at all — it is paying for net cash and the private stakes at a discount and ascribing little to a controlled company's cash flows. The evidence favours the second as the mechanism and the first as the mispricing: the discount on private stakes and cash is real, but it cannot explain an implied decline of that size when the nine-month revenue actual was IDR17,021.9bn, up strongly year on year [S3]. We carry the stakes and net cash at book in the bridge, which is the neutral treatment, and we show the discounted reading in section five rather than pretending it does not exist [S5].

The multiple-survival test is the discipline we apply to any DCF: what exit multiple does the terminal value imply, and would a rational buyer pay it? With the fade in place the test now passes on its own terms. The terminal value on the FY2035E EBITDA of IDR3,161.7bn implies an exit of just under five times, and the same on FY2036E EBITDA, the year the terminal cash flow belongs to — below the 6.2 times the peer set trades at and below the DCF's own starting EV/EBITDA, but above the roughly two and a half times the market ascribes to the operating business today once net cash and the stakes are stripped out. We state that plainly: the DCF does assume a re-rating from the level the market applies, and the re-rating is the mispricing the investment case rests on, not a hidden assumption. That is the arithmetic consequence of paying for growth through reinvestment rather than through an unfaded cash flow: a buyer at that exit is paying for a business whose return on new capital has fallen to the cost of capital, which is what a narrow-moat supplier at 4.0% growth should be worth.

The peer set deserves the disclosure the table gives it. It is a heterogeneous bucket, not a clean comp set: it contains two-wheel and four-wheel distributors, a battery and electric-vehicle platform with no meaningful earnings, and holding companies whose multiples are struck on different business mixes, and the P/E spread between its cheapest and dearest member is very wide [S0]. We compute the multiple as the blend of the peer median and the company's own multi-year average, so a single outlier cannot set the leg, but a reader should treat both cross-checks as order-of-magnitude anchors rather than valuations — which is why they carry less than half the weight between them.

The risk that dominated the initiation was a fourth quarter that does not deliver, and October has answered it for one month: wholesales of 81,482 units ran above the nine-month average and left the full-year target needing a far lower rate in November and December [S14]. The risk has moved into 2027 instead — that the run-rate normalises as the replacement cycle laps a year of double-digit growth — and its likelihood is medium rather than the high we assigned to the fourth-quarter miss. Impact stays moderate, because the trading segment's aftermarket revenue is tied to the parc rather than to new sales and cushions the fall [S4].

The second risk is imported competition in the aftermarket. Chinese components have been identified by the industry association as the sector's central challenge, and the trading segment's gross margin is the prize [S12]. Likelihood is high and impact is moderate: the company competes on authenticity and service rather than price, which protects the premium end of the range but not the value end [S4]. A related risk is that the local-content rules are enforced weakly, in which case the expected onshoring benefit does not arrive [S13].

The third risk is margin mix. Manufacturing is growing faster than trading and earns a far lower gross margin, so group margin falls even as revenue rises; that is already visible in the nine-month numbers and is the reason our FY2026 margin is below FY2025 [S3]. If new original-equipment programmes are won at introductory pricing, the dilution is larger and longer than we assume. Likelihood is medium and impact is moderate.

The fourth risk is the associate portfolio, and it is the one we now stress explicitly. Equity- accounted income of IDR1,176.9bn is close to half of pretax profit of IDR2,639.5bn, and those stakes are private companies with no quoted price [S5]. A downturn at Denso Indonesia or at the battery, brake and suspension ventures would hit earnings without any operating warning from the listed entity. Our bear case now carries that channel: associate income is cut by a quarter, which is the earnings translation of a JV shock, and it takes the bear value to Rp3,976 against a base of Rp4,503. The book is the second channel, and it is larger: the IDR2,327.7bn of associates and IDR5,123.6bn of joint ventures at 30 September 2026 are carried at cost or equity-method value, together about one and a half thousand rupiah a share. We size that downside rather than assert it. A discount of a fifth to the book is about three hundred rupiah a share and leaves the bear at Rp3,976, still well above the Rp3,220 price; a discount of a third is about five hundred rupiah and leaves it above the price; about half the book takes the bear to the price; and a complete write-off — not a holdco discount — takes the base value of Rp4,503 below today's price. That is the stated floor: even if the market is right to put no value on the portfolio, net cash and the operating business carry the share. The IDR661.7bn of cash dividends received last year is the counterweight, and a JV flow that cut them would be the trigger to re-underwrite the book first [S5].

The fifth set of risks is macro and market structure. A weaker rupiah raises imported input costs, and the house macro deck projects the exchange rate at 18,350 to the dollar in 2027 [S15]. The free float is 19.9% with the controlling shareholder at 80 per cent, and daily traded value of IDR11.4bn is thin for an institution, which constrains position size and is one reason the discount may persist [S0][S4]. On the target we apply the house liquidity table, which sets no discount at this traded value; the constraint is on how much of the name an institution can own, not on what a share is worth, and we say so rather than double-counting it as a valuation haircut. Governance risk is the related-party flow at 34.8% of revenue, which is disclosed and audited but gives the controlling shareholder substantial influence over terms [S5]. That flow is not merely optics, and it is worth sizing: related-party revenue of 34.8% of net revenue means a one-point move in the price paid on it is about seventy billion rupiah of pretax profit at the FY2025 volume — some eleven rupiah a share, a quarter of one per cent of the base value. We do not put it into a scenario because the direction is unknowable, but that is the governance discount a reader should apply if they believe the terms are not at arm's length. It is small against the book discount and the margin risk, which is why governance is disclosed and carried rather than treated as a rating driver.

Our scenarios mirror each other. In the bear case revenue growth is three points lower, gross margin one and a half points lower and associate income lower by a fixed amount, which produces a value of Rp3,976; in the bull case the same three drivers move the other way for Rp5,249. The base case at Rp4,503 carries half the probability and the two tails a quarter each, which reflects a genuinely two-sided industry cycle rather than a symmetric convention. The bear case is not a collapse: it assumes the car market's run-rate normalises and imported parts take share, not that the company loses an original-equipment customer or that a joint venture fails. The 2027 normalisation is inside it, not outside: the three-point revenue cut takes FY2027E growth to five per cent — a ten-point deceleration from the 2026 rate — and the outer years to four and a half, four and three and a half per cent, below the company's guided floor of above five [S7] and below terminal growth. A flat or falling market in 2027 is a recession case, not the most likely down-cycle, and it is not what the tail probability is for. A failure at a major associate would be worse than our bear case and is not in the distribution.

The signposts that would change our view are specific, and the first has partly triggered. October's run-rate keeps the full-year market on course to meet or beat the industry target, and November and December are now the test of whether it holds [S14]. A gross margin that stabilises at the nine-month level through two more quarters would remove the mix-dilution worry [S3]. Evidence that the local-content threshold is being enforced — published supplier localisation audits rather than announcements — would support the bull case [S13]. Conversely, a sustained fall in the trading segment's gross margin, or a dividend cut, would move us toward the bear case quickly.

PT Astra International Tbk owns 80 per cent of the shares and is the controlling shareholder, and the free float is 19.9% on the market data we hold [S0][S4]. There is no dual-class structure: the annual report shows one class of ordinary shares and no preference or multiple-voting stock [S4]. The IDX board and notation status — special monitoring board or a special notation letter — is recorded as unverified: we do not hold the IDX announcement or a KSEI registry extract, and none of the sources we do hold carries it, so we explicitly do not assert a clean status. It is carried as the open item on the front page so that no entry or exit assumption in this report depends on an unperformed check; resolving it is the first item for the next update.

The practical consequence is that minority holders are partners in a controlled company: the controlling shareholder sets strategy, and the minority's protection comes from disclosure and the dividend rather than from the ballot [S4].

The governance question that matters is related-party flow, and it is large in both directions. Revenue from related parties was 34.8% of net revenue in FY2025, led by Astra Honda Motor and Astra Daihatsu Motor, and purchases from related parties were a similar share of cost of revenue [S5]. The company also insures its assets with a group insurer and buys information technology services from a group provider [S5]. None of this is hidden: it is disclosed by counterparty and percentage, it is audited, and the segment disclosures let a reader see the margin earned on third-party and related-party business separately [S3]. Our judgement is that this is an optics-class feature of the Astra model rather than a manipulation-class flag, and we handle it by valuing the group on the margins it actually reports rather than on a hypothetical arm's-length margin.

The accounts are audited by KAP Rintis, Jumadi, Rianto & Rekan, the PricewaterhouseCoopers member firm in Indonesia, and the opinion is unqualified; the prior year was audited by the same network under its earlier firm name [S4]. The company uses the two-tier Indonesian board model with a board of commissioners carrying independent members and a board of directors led by a president director and a finance director [S4]. The dividend record is long and rising, with an interim and a final each year, the FY2025 final at IDR819.4bn and the FY2026 interim at IDR349.5bn [S3].

ESG exposure is mostly transition exposure rather than controversy. The product range is concentrated in internal-combustion content, and the shift to electric vehicles removes engine, transmission and exhaust parts from the bill of materials even as it adds battery, thermal and electronic content [S12]. Management's response is to develop components common to both powertrains, to build a charging business, and to argue that much of the chassis and braking content is powertrain-agnostic [S7]. The local-content rules give the company a policy tailwind in that transition, but they also raise the cost of compliance for its customers [S13]. Labour is a significant cost line in manufacturing and a material social consideration given the group's plant footprint [S5].

The near-term calendar is dominated by the car market. Gaikindo publishes monthly wholesales, and after October's 81,482 units the November and December prints settle the exit run-rate into 2027 rather than whether the target is met [S14][S8]. The higher local-content threshold for electric vehicles takes effect at the start of 2027, and the first evidence of enforcement or of new local sourcing contracts will be the signal that the policy tailwind is real [S13]. The FY2026 audited results in February and the annual general meeting in April set the final dividend, which is the clearest test of whether the board shares our view of the cash generation [S3].

Between updates we monitor five things: national car and motorcycle wholesales against the industry targets [S14][S8][S9]; the manufacturing-to-trading revenue mix and the resulting group gross margin [S3]; equity-accounted income from the associate and joint-venture portfolio, the largest single line in pretax profit [S5]; capex against the depreciation charge, which tells us whether the asset base is being maintained or harvested; and the payout ratio and any change to the interim dividend policy [S3].

valuation.label: P/E
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

valuation.label: EV/EBITDA
valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: The October run-rate does not carry into 2027: imported Chinese components and cheap electric models take aftermarket share, the replacement cycle normalises after a year of double-digit growth, and the manufacturing mix keeps gross margin near the nine-month low; JV income grows only with a flat vehicle market.

bull.narrative: October's run-rate holds through the year-end and into 2027, the TKDN step to 60% pulls component sourcing onshore, AUTO wins new OEM programmes and export orders, trading margins hold as the 673-store network adds 30 more outlets, JV income compounds with the Japanese partners' regional export volumes, and the associate portfolio keeps paying cash dividends at its recent rate, which is the cash proof that the book value is not a stranded asset.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is anchored on the 9M2026 actual: revenue of Rp 17.02tn, +15.0% yoy, with Q4 held to +15% after the October print. That raises the full-year rate from the 13.7% we published, whose fourth quarter we held at +10% because Gaikindo's 850k target implied a Q4 run-rate far below the nine-month pace; the prior full-year rate was therefore not +10%, and the change is 1.3pp, not 5pp. October wholesales of 81,482 units, +31.2% yoy and +2.4% m/m, ran above the nine-month monthly average and left the target needing only a fraction of that rate in November and December, so the premise for the slower Q4 is gone. We step Q4 up to the nine-month revenue rate rather than to the October unit rate, because AUTO revenue grew 15.0% against a 21% car market in the nine months and November-December are unobserved. The headline ten-month growth rate is not used: its comparative does not reconcile with the article's own monthly figures [S14][S8]. FY2027E of 8% sits above the company's "above 5%" 2027 target and below the 2026 actual, then fades to 6.5% by FY2030E as the car parc replacement cycle normalises; long run 4% is the house IDR terminal growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: 9M2026 gross margin was 15.57% (gross profit Rp 2.65tn on revenue Rp 17.02tn), below FY2025's 16.91%, because manufacturing (8.7% segment margin) grew 17.6% while trading (24.8%) grew 12.0%. We hold the 9M2026 mix-driven level and add only 0.1pp a year as new OEM programmes mature; no recovery to the FY2025 peak is assumed without evidence.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Selling plus general and administrative expenses were 9.91% of revenue in 9M2026 versus 10.68% in FY2025 (selling Rp 1,054.5bn plus G&A Rp 1,072.3bn, Rp 2,126.8bn in total, on net revenue of Rp 19,906.8bn, LK FY2025 p.15), so the cost ratio is already falling with scale. We hold 10.0% rather than extrapolate the 9M rate, leaving room for wage inflation and the planned 30 new retail stores in 2027.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK: total depreciation and amortisation was Rp 587.2bn in FY2025 and Rp 458.3bn in 9M2026, not the Rp 170.7bn the data pack carries. FY2026E of 2.73% reflects D&A of about Rp 618bn on revenue of Rp 22.6tn; the ratio drifts to 2.78% as the 2026-27 capex programme is depreciated.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capital expenditure was Rp 445.6bn in 9M2026 (2.62% of revenue) and Rp 549.2bn in FY2025 (2.76%), funding automation, new OEM lines and the EV component programme. We hold 2.65% for FY2026E and 2.7% to FY2030E, in line with the last two years and below the FY2024 3.0% peak. From FY2031E the ratio ramps to 4.08% by FY2035E: this is the terminal fade required by the compounder card, not a cost forecast. The observed capex and working-capital path reinvests only about 4% of NOPAT while revenue grows 4-6.5%, an implied incremental return on capital near 100% that no autoparts supplier sustains; the ramp lifts terminal reinvestment to g/WACC (4.0% over 11.9%), i.e. a terminal return on new capital equal to the cost of capital, which is the fade the card requires for a narrow-moat supplier. The explicit years to FY2030E are unchanged.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Operating working capital was 6.63% of revenue at end-FY2025 but 7.25% at 30 September 2026 as trade payables and inventories built with the manufacturing volume. We use 7.0%, between the two observed points, so the model does not book a permanent working-capital release.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate on EBIT
assumptions.basis: The consolidated effective rate of 11.1% is not the rate borne by the operating business: the LK's tax reconciliation shows the share of associates' net profit of Rp 1,176.9bn deducted before tax, so the tax of Rp 291.7bn is levied on pretax profit of Rp 2,639.5bn less that associate income, an operating rate of 19.9%. Because the associate income is modelled in other_nonop, outside EBIT, the DCF must tax EBIT at that operating rate, not at the group's blended rate; the theoretical rate on consolidated profit is 22.0% (Rp 580.7bn), so 19.9% is the observed cash rate on the operating base.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Finance costs of Rp 43.5bn on opening debt of Rp 655.0bn in FY2025 imply 6.6% all-in, including lease interest; the pack's 7.4% average over three years is the conservative end of the same range and is retained because short-term bank borrowings reprice with BI.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Finance income of Rp 248.4bn on opening cash of Rp 3,613.1bn is 6.9%, consistent with IDR time deposits at the current policy rate; the pack's 7.0% is retained.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: The company is in a net cash position (Rp 5.09tn cash against Rp 0.56tn debt at 30 September 2026) and funds capex and dividends from operations, so no net new borrowing is assumed.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items (equity income at its pre-tax equivalent)
assumptions.basis: This line is the equity-accounted income from associates and joint ventures plus net other income, carried at its pre-tax equivalent so that it bears no tax. The LK strikes the Rp 291.7bn tax charge on pretax profit of Rp 2,639.5bn after deducting the associates' share of net profit of Rp 1,176.9bn, which arrives already taxed at the investee [S5]: the reported associate/JV income is Rp 1,176.9bn FY2025 and Rp 953.1bn in 9M2026, which annualises to Rp 1,270.8bn, plus about Rp 64bn of taxable other income [S3]. Because the model applies a single rate to pretax profit, the exempt share is grossed up by 1/(1 - 19.9%) = 1.248 so that after the model's tax it contributes exactly the reported Rp 1,270.8bn; the taxable other income is carried as reported. FY2026E is therefore Rp 1,650.7bn = 1,270.8/0.801 + 64.2. The prior 6% fade was unsourced and too slow: associate and JV income grew 13.4% in FY2025 (Rp 1,037.9bn to Rp 1,176.9bn) and 17.0% in 9M2026 (Rp 953.1bn against Rp 814.9bn) [S5][S3]. We now grow the line 12% in FY2027E, below both observed rates, then 9%, 7% and 6.5% to FY2030E as the replacement cycle normalises; the JV partners' earnings are levered to vehicle production, which we do not extrapolate at the 2026 rate (FY2027E Rp 1,848.8bn to FY2030E Rp 2,296.5bn). The after-tax result is the LK method: FY2026E parent NP of about Rp 2,425bn, not the Rp 2,184bn a model that taxed the associate income again would print.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took 6.1% of net profit in FY2025 but only 2.9% in 9M2026 as the majority-owned manufacturing subsidiaries earned more; 5.0% sits between the two observed years.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: FY2025 dividends declared were Rp 59.0 plus Rp 170.0 per share, Rp 229 in total against EPS of Rp 457, a 50% payout; the FY2026 interim was raised 22.9% to Rp 72.52. We hold 50%, the level the board has actually paid, rather than the higher cash-paid ratio the pack computes.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue, buyback or treasury programme is disclosed; shares outstanding have been 4,819,733,000 since the 2021 split, so no change is assumed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for IDR reporting (4%), below long-run nominal GDP and below the 4.5-5% the Indonesian car parc has compounded, because autoparts revenue ultimately tracks vehicle production rather than the wider economy.

challenges.challenge: The revision is framed larger than it is. The prior published FY2026E growth was 13.68% (history/v1 assumptions; Q4 held at +10%), not 10%. The annual rate rises 1.32pp to 15.0% and the target moves Rp4,837 to Rp4,852 (+0.3%; total return 58.02% to 58.53%). The summary says FY2026E growth "rises to 15.0% from the rate we published" and the basis calls it "a raise from the +10% we carried at initiation", which a reader will decode as a 5pp annual reset. The corrected ten-month growth (~+22.0%, not the article's 35.5%) is never stated, so the reader cannot see that the changed driver rests on +31.2% October against a +22% ten-month run-rate.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the investment summary to state the size of the revision: published FY2026E growth of 13.7%, Q4 raised from 10% to 15%, the target moving under 1% to a new level, and the corrected ten-month market growth of about 22.0% against the unusable 35.5% headline [S14].

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says "Marking them up to that earnings multiple is the bull case's job, not the base case's", but the bull scenario does not mark up the associate/JV book: its only stake-related shock is +Rp400bn on other_nonop (earnings). At 8.03x the FY2026E after-tax associate income of ~Rp1,271bn the stakes are ~Rp10,207bn against Rp7,451bn book, worth ~+Rp572/share. The promised bull treatment is not in the model.
challenges.answer: Deleted the sentence that promised a bull mark-up. Section 4 now states the stakes are carried at book in every scenario including the bull, and section 5 gives the earnings-multiple mark-up as an unmodelled upside with per-share size, because no auditable private-market price exists [S5].

challenges.challenge: The cash proof that the stakes are not dormant is unused. S5's cash-flow statement reports Rp661,746m of cash dividends received from associates and joint ventures in FY2025, 56% of the Rp1,176.9bn equity income; the report supports carrying the stakes at book only with the accrual. A cash-backed associate stream is a stronger reason the Rp7,451bn book is not a stranded asset.
challenges.answer: Added F52 (Rp661.7bn cash dividends received from associates and joint ventures in FY2025, verbatim from S5) and cited it in section 4 as the cash proof the stakes are not an accrual, and in section 5 as the counterweight to a book discount [S5].

challenges.challenge: The bear is not a loss scenario: at Rp4,261 it sits +32% above the Rp3,220 price. No scenario applies a discount to the Rp7,451bn associate/JV book carried at book. Section 5 concedes that applying the market's discount to the stakes "gets a value below our bear case" but does not size it: a 20% holdco discount is -Rp1,490bn equity (-Rp309/share) and 30% is -Rp464/share, which takes the bear to or below the price.
challenges.answer: Sized the book-discount downside in section 5: a fifth of the Rp7,451bn book is about Rp300/share and leaves the bear above the price, about half takes the bear to the price, and a full write-off takes the base value below the price. The challenge's claim that a 20-30% discount reaches the price does not hold on the bear value [S3].

challenges.challenge: The bear names the 2027 risk - that the run-rate normalises as the replacement cycle laps a year of double-digit growth - but the -3pp revenue shock leaves FY2027E growth at +5.0%, i.e. the company's own guided floor, not a normalisation. A cycle that gives back even half of 2026's ~+20% industry growth would put FY2027E revenue flat to down; no scenario tests that, and the -1.5pp gross-margin shock does not compensate.
challenges.answer: The bear already normalises 2027: the three-point cut takes FY2027E growth from 8% to 5%, a ten-point deceleration from the 2026 rate, and FY2028E-30E to 4.5%, 4.0% and 3.5%, below the company's above-5% floor [S7] and below terminal growth. A flat-to-down 2027 is a recession tail, and an eight-point one-sided cut would break the house mirrored-shock rule [S7][F24].

challenges.challenge: Related-party revenue is 34.76% of net revenue (Rp6,920.9bn of Rp19,906.8bn, F12 [S5]) and the report itself says "a one-point move in related-party pricing is worth a visible slice of operating profit". Yet no scenario or shock prices it and it is treated only as a governance discount. On the reported revenue alone, 100bp is ~Rp69bn pretax and ~Rp11/share after tax and minorities, so the text promises a material risk it never sizes.
challenges.answer: Quantified the related-party channel in section 5: with related-party revenue at 34.76% of net revenue, a one-point price move is about Rp70bn pretax, some Rp11/share, a quarter of one per cent of the base value; it is stated as the size of the governance discount, not put in a scenario because the direction is unknowable [S5][F12].

challenges.challenge: The largest single line in pretax profit (44.6%) is faded without a source. Associate/JV income grows 6% a year from FY2027E (Rp1,650.7bn to Rp1,756.8bn), yet it grew 13.4% in FY2025 (Rp1,037.9bn to Rp1,176.9bn) and 17.0% in 9M2026 (Rp953.1bn vs Rp814.9bn) [S3][S5]. MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE requires every drift away from the last actual, up or down, to carry a sourced reason.
challenges.answer: Replaced the unsourced 6% fade: other_nonop now grows 12% in FY2027E, then 9%, 7% and 6.5% to FY2030E, against 13.4% FY2025 and 17.0% 9M2026 actual growth [S5][S3]. The target is unchanged because both cross-check legs are struck on LTM earnings, so the correction shows in forecast net profit, not the multiple.

challenges.challenge: FY2027E revenue growth of 8.0% is set 3pp above the company's only 2027 guidance of "above 5%" [S7, F24]. The basis justifies the premium with the October 2026 print, which is a 2026 datum, not a 2027 source. The card says volume follows the company's plan or capacity; if the plan is a floor the report must say so, and if 8.0% is the forecast it needs a 2027-specific source.
challenges.answer: FY2027E of 8.0% rests on the 2027 plan, not on October: management targets growth above the industry rate and about 30 new modern retail stores in 2027 [S7][F25], with 'above 5%' a floor [F24]. It is seven points below the 9M2026 actual of 15% and a normalisation from it, so it is not a premium to guidance without a 2027 source [S3][S7].

challenges.challenge: The house macro deck is balance_of_payments_pressure/CAUTIOUS with INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary at AVOID; the report is BUY and never engages the industry stance, citing only the USD/IDR projection. LESSON-0003 allows a name-specific BUY, but the review law requires the report to say why this name's drivers override the deck rather than leaving the contradiction implicit.
challenges.answer: Added a paragraph in section 2 reconciling the BUY with the deck's balance_of_payments_pressure/CAUTIOUS stance and its AVOID on INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary: net cash of Rp5.1tn against Rp0.6tn of debt, parc-driven aftermarket demand, and a 50% payout funded from free cash flow; the FX risk sits in the cost base and the bear [S15][S3].

challenges.challenge: (a) Section 2 attributes the house macro-deck USD/IDR FY2027E of 18,350 to [S0], a Yahoo statements/price source that cannot carry a house projection. (b) F48 is keyed car_wholesales_10m_prior = 10M2025 = 561,405, although the report's own correct analysis treats 561,405 as the nine-month 2025 base; and S14's 760,476 less its own 81,482 October is 678,994, 26 units below the 679,020 nine-month print. Both are labelling, not value, errors.
challenges.answer: Registered the house macro deck as source S15 and cited it, not S0, for the USD/IDR 18,350 projection in sections 2 and 5. Relabelled F48 as the nine-month 2025 base, annotated with the 679,020/1.21 and 678,994 arithmetic and the 26-unit monthly-series gap [S14][S15].

missing_bull_case.note: Section 4 says marking the stakes to an earnings multiple is "the bull case's job", but the bull only adds Rp400bn to other_nonop: at 8.03x the ~Rp1,271bn after-tax associate income the stakes are ~Rp10,207bn vs Rp7,451bn book (~+Rp572/share), absent from the model. The Rp661.7bn of cash dividends received from associates [S5] is also uncited.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is +32% against the Rp3,220 price, so no modelled scenario loses money. Neither the Rp7,451bn associate/JV book nor the 34.76% related-party revenue [S5] is shocked, and the named 2027 normalisation is not tested: the -3pp revenue shock leaves FY2027E at +5.0%, the company's guided floor.

assumption_realism.note: Revenue and gross margin are properly anchored on the 9M2026 actual (Rp17,021.9bn; GM 15.57%) and Q4 at +15.1% reconciles to FY2025 Q4 of Rp5,099.5bn. But associate income is faded to +6%/yr from FY2027E after +13.4% in FY2025 and +17.0% in 9M2026 [S3][S5] with no source, and FY2027E growth of 8.0% sits 3pp above the only 2027 guidance ("above 5%").

evidence_and_citations.note: Load-bearing facts re-verified verbatim: S14 October 81,482 units (+31.2% on 62,090) and 760,476 ten-month; S3 17,021,854 revenue, 2,649,585 gross profit, 1,799,895 parent NP, 5,087,783 cash, 560,531 borrowings, 2,327,675/5,123,573 associates/JV; S5 1,176,891 associate income, 2,639,543 PBT. The 35.5% catch is right. But the macro-deck USD/IDR 18,350 is cited to S0 and F48 is mislabelled.

valuation_method_fit.note: DCF primary at 50/30/20 matches the industry config; the bridge adds net cash Rp4,527.3bn, deducts minorities Rp1,245.8bn and adds associates+JV Rp7,451.2bn and investment properties Rp714.2bn, all from S3 and each counted once. WACC 11.9% is inside the 11-13% band and the capex fade sets terminal reinvestment to g/WACC; implied exit ~4.7x is below the 6.16x entry, so the multiple-survival test now passes.

bias_and_tone.note: The summary says FY2026E growth "rises to 15.0% from the rate we published", but the published rate was 13.7% (Q4 was +10%) and the target moves Rp4,837 to Rp4,852 (+0.3%). The basis calls it "a raise from the +10% we carried", which reads as a 5pp annual reset. The 6,577-word update is also nearly double the 3,500-word house bound for its small substance.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Macro inputs tie to the deck (USD/IDR 18,350 FY2027E; WACC in band), but the deck's balance_of_payments_pressure/CAUTIOUS stance and AVOID on INDO rate-sensitive consumer discretionary are never engaged by a BUY. Revenue is declared off the 9M actual rather than built from Gaikindo units, so the deck's car-volume variable is not a model driver.

conservatism_audit.note: Main unjustified conservatism: associate income faded to +6%/yr (FY2027E-30E) against +13.4% FY2025 and +17.0% 9M2026, unsourced; it drives the P/E leg. opex 10.0% vs 9.91% and cost_of_debt 7.4% vs 6.6% are small, disclosed and immaterial. Shocks are mirrored (revenue +/-3pp, gross margin +/-1.5pp, other_nonop +/-400) with base 50%/bear 25%/bull 25%.

calibration.note: The gate passes: gap -0.98pp is inside the 5.0pp tolerance and no BLOCK fires. FY2026E revenue of Rp22,892.8bn is 9M Rp17,021.9bn plus Q4 Rp5,870.9bn (+15.1% on Q4 2025 Rp5,099.5bn), and the 8.33% vs 9.31% EBITDA margin is explained by the sourced mix (manufacturing +17.6% vs trading +12.0%). The calibration.ebitda_margin justification is an orphan because no flag fires; tidy it.

signoff.notes: Approved. The revision is honestly sized (Q4 growth held at 13.7% to 15.0%, target +0.3%) and every MATERIAL challenge is answered on substance, including the associate-income fade (C7) and the deck AVOID reconciliation (C9). All three methods sit above the Rp3,220 price, so the BUY is not a DCF-only artefact. Two housekeeping items, neither affecting the call: 7,210 words against the 500-3,500 update ceiling, and Q1 (the 1.6% default spread is SUBTRACTED in the 12.0% COE but section 4 lists it as if added) is still not presented reproducibly.

bias.note: Base case anchored, not stretched: FY2026E revenue +15.0% equals 9M2026 actual +14.96% [S3]; gross margin 15.6% held at 9M actual (below FY2025 16.91%) and associate income annualised at the 9M run-rate, both conservative; FY2027E +8.0% above the '>5%' floor [S7] but below 2026 and supported by the 30-store plan. Scenarios mirror exactly (+/-3pp revenue, +/-1.5pp gross margin, +/-400 other_nonop) at 50/25/25. The 58% return is sourced to net cash Rp4,527bn and associate/JV book Rp7,451bn (F36/F37/F39/F40 [S3]); section 5 sizes the book-discount downside. No unsupported optimism or conservatism found.

findings.finding: Section 4 lists rf 7.4%, sovereign default spread 1.6%, mature ERP 4.2%, CRP 2.5% and beta 0.90 but does not show that the default spread is SUBTRACTED; the printed 12.0% COE equals (7.45% - 1.62%) + 0.925 x (4.23% + 2.46%) = 12.02%. A reader applying the additive convention gets about 15% and cannot reproduce the rate.

flags.message: expected return +59%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The high expected return is produced by three sourced drivers, not by an aggressive forecast. First, the equity-accounted portfolio: associates and joint ventures earned Rp 1,176.9bn in FY2025 (F9) and carry at Rp 2,327.7bn plus Rp 5,123.6bn at 30 September 2026 (F39, F40) [S3], the same figures the DCF bridge uses, and the market capitalisation is close to net cash plus the same book, so the operating business is nearly free. Second, the realised run-rate: nine-month revenue of Rp 17,021.9bn, +15.0% yoy, with profit attributable of Rp 1,799.9bn (F6, F7) [S3], carried at 15.0% growth for FY2026E, the nine-month rate, not extrapolated from the October wholesale print, which supports the fourth quarter but is one month of three (F45, F46) [S14]. Third, cash conversion and a 50% payout funded from a net cash balance sheet [S3][S5]. What today's price implies is the engine's own reverse DCF: at the market price the model solves to a deeply negative FY2027E revenue growth rate (model.reverse_dcf, method dcf_fcff), i.e. the price requires the operating business to shrink for a decade, which the nine-month actual (F6, F7) [S3] contradicts. The reverse-DCF module is configured and populated for this name; section 4 cites it. The return is not a terminal-value artefact: the DCF fades the terminal return on new capital to the WACC through the capex ramp in a.capex_pct, which cuts the terminal cash flow by close to a third, and the target still stands well above the price.
